request.title: Studio Original 001 — agents' choice
request.prompt: The player tried Neon Salvage and honestly did not like it. The studio is commissioned to create an ENTIRELY NEW game. The user's whole creative brief is: MOBILE. LIGHT. SIMPLE. FUN. Let the studio decide the concept, real game name, theme, visual style, mechanics, challenge, scoring and session length. The game ID and request title are administrative placeholders, not a required creative name: choose your own name for the actual game. Do not ask the player to choose concepts. Record the concept the council selected and why its moment-to-moment interaction should be enjoyable. Build a genuinely different core loop, not a reskin or extension of Neon Salvage. Prioritize an immediately understandable, satisfying interaction and easy replay over feature count. Use the existing mobile game host and interface contract, with responsive one-finger play. Keep it self-contained and quick to load: combined index.html/game.js/game.css at most 200,000 bytes; no external assets, libraries, services, accounts or downloads. Do not change any existing game. Implement the actual game and its end/replay loop. The coding agent must run concrete game-specific checks for its chosen scoring/progression and end conditions, in addition to the independent mobile gate. Explain what the checks actually prove; whether the player finds it fun remains a playtest question. Complete the tested publication to a new stable play URL.
acceptance: The studio chooses and implements an original concept and real game name. The actual page presents that name and one short, clear instruction; no creative selection is passed back to the player.
The new game's core loop is meaningfully different from Neon Salvage, with a clear player action, immediate understandable feedback, a goal or challenge and a repeatable end/replay loop.
Mobile portrait play is usable at 390x844 and 360x780, with one-finger controls, readable UI, reachable buttons and no horizontal overflow or accidental page scrolling during gameplay.
The combined HTML/CSS/JS is at most 200,000 bytes and runs entirely from local game files without external libraries, assets, accounts, network services or downloads.
Touch start, actual player interaction, pause/resume, pointer cancellation, clean restart and replay work. The visible score or progress corresponds to real game state.

The coding agent executes and reports concrete checks of its chosen scoring/progression and success/failure or end conditions, plus syntax checking. The independent mobile acceptance and independent QA must pass before publication.
Publish to a new game URL, preserve all existing games, retain the accepted source and evidence, and verify the exact live files.

producer.claim: Scope the job to create a small, original, mobile arcade game named 'Peach Bounce' with a distinct core loop fully contained in under 200KB HTML/CSS/JS bundle, playable with one-finger controls in portrait mode on standard mobile viewports.
producer.rationale: The studio selected 'Peach Bounce' as the new game concept, featuring a simple interaction: bouncing a peach into jam tiles. This differs meaningfully from Neon Salvage, focusing on immediate, understandable feedback, a scoring objective, and short repeatable rounds fitting the brief of mobile, light, simple, and fun. The playable result must meet all interface, size, and operational requirements per the game contract, including start/pause/restart buttons, visible score, player position feedback, and proper game state transitions.
producer.objections: Potential uncertainties include whether the chosen 'Peach Bounce' concept truly offers a 'fun' experience for players, as enjoyment is subjective and not guaranteed by compliance with technical requirements. There may be edge cases in touch handling or viewport sizes not fully covered. The byte size limit may constrain possible features or polish.
producer.proposed_action: Define 'Peach Bounce' playable scope as: a single-page HTML5 canvas game allowing one-finger drag to control a tray bouncing a peach, attempting to hit 15 jam tile targets per round. Provide a clear game title and one-line start instruction on the main page. Implement start, pause/resume, and restart controls with visible score and elapsed time, reporting player position. The game ends after all tiles are hit or a fixed time limit; then allows immediate replay. Verify all controls work on 390x844 and 360x780 portrait viewports with no overflow or scroll. Confirm combined code size under 200,000 bytes. Produce concrete JS checks of scoring and end conditions, pause behavior, and snapshot consistency. Await independent mobile acceptance and QA testing before publishing with stable play URL.
producer.required_evidence: Evidence should include: 1) A public stable playable URL demonstrating the game running as specified on standard mobile viewports with proper UI and one-finger control. 2) Executed automated tests proving compliance with scoring, progression, pause/resume, restart, and viewport requirements. 3) Byte size verification report of the combined HTML/CSS/JS bundle under 200KB. 4) Screenshots or logs showing game mode transitions ('ready', 'running', 'paused', 'over') and snapshot object exposing real-time state. 5) Independent acceptance test results confirming no scroll overflow, reachable buttons, and input responsiveness. 6) Evidence of code syntax checks passing (e.g. node --check game.js). 7) Confirmation that existing games remain unchanged and all requested job criteria are satisfied before final publication.

designer.claim: The core loop of 'Peach Bounce' involves the player using one-finger drag to control a tray that bounces a peach onto jam tiles, aiming to hit all targets within a set time. The game provides immediate feedback through dynamic peach and tray movement, score updates when jam tiles are hit, and visual state transitions. Mobile controls are simplified to a single finger drag moving the tray horizontally at the bottom of the screen, keeping interaction intuitive and reachable in portrait mode. Feedback includes visible score, elapsed time, clear start/pause/restart buttons, and snapshot state exposure to comply with the game contract.
designer.rationale: The chosen mechanics deliver a light, simple, and fun mobile experience that is distinct from Neon Salvage by focusing on a different player action (dragging tray to bounce rather than other mechanics). One-finger horizontal drag is immediately understandable and effortless to use on small screens, minimizing cognitive and motor load. The bouncing peach and jam tiles provide satisfying cause-and-effect feedback, encouraging short play sessions with a clear goal of hitting all jam tiles or beating the timer. The UI layout ensures all controls and feedback elements remain visible and reachable without accidental scrolling or obliterating gameplay space, complying with the acceptance criteria.
designer.objections: While the core loop and control scheme aligns with the brief, actual player enjoyment is not guaranteed without playtesting since 'fun' is subjective. The fixed-size jam tile layout and bounce physics may feel repetitive if not polished. Potential edge cases with touch responsiveness or accessibility across all mobile portrait resolutions could arise. The byte-size limit restricts adding richer visual or audio feedback that might increase immersion. Current evidence does not verify physical-device testing or long-term engagement metrics.

critic.claim: The 'Peach Bounce' plan may fail in critical areas including unresponsive game start, false progress indication, inadequate touch input handling, improper pause/resume behavior, clean restart issues, viewport overflow, unbalanced gameplay, and missing prompt-required UI elements.
critic.rationale: While the plan details a concept consistent with the brief and contract, several assumptions remain unverified. The start control must respond only to genuine user taps, not touch cancel or spurious events, or else the game might appear unresponsive or start unpredictably. Showing progress (score/time) must reflect actual game state—not fabricated or desynchronized values—to prevent fake progress illusions. The one-finger drag control must robustly handle various touch edge cases (pointer cancellation, multiple touches, accidental gestures) or the tray control could become unresponsive or jittery. Pause and resume must freeze and continue elapsed time precisely, maintaining snapshot integrity; failure causes gameplay confusion. Restart must reset all transient states without residue, ensuring a clean fresh session. UI must adapt perfectly to tested mobile viewports (390x844, 360x780) without horizontal overflow, accidental page scrolling, or unreachable controls; failures degrade usability. Core loop balance (bounce physics, jam tile difficulty, timer) needs empirical verification to avoid trivial or frustrating sessions. The prompt demands a visible named game title and single succinct instruction shown on start; omission here is a contract breach causing user confusion.
critic.objections: The current plan rationales rely heavily on assumptions about touch input robustness across devices and viewport sizes without physical-device or full QA approval evidence. The byte size constraint may force compromises in input smoothing and visual feedback that impact usability. Playtesting is required to confirm the subjective 'fun' aspect and balance. Early remarks note circular approval delays and lack of physical device verification, indicating existing uncertainty and incomplete validation of these critical concerns.

coder_report:
# Peach Bounce — implementation handoff

Implemented the council-selected **Peach Bounce** in the new isolated directory `docs/games/studio-original-001/`. No existing game, metadata, test, dependency, workflow, or publishing code was edited. Source files are `index.html`, `game.css`, and `game.js`.

## Concept and behavior

Drag a wide tray horizontally to bounce a peach into 15 jam tiles. Tray impact position controls the outgoing angle. Each tile awards exactly one point. Clear all 15 within 75 simulation seconds to win; timeout ends the round with the achieved score. Missing the tray returns a fresh peach without awarding points, keeping the interaction forgiving. Immediate tile disappearance, jam flecks, peach bounces, score updates and clear end messages make action and result understandable. This is a paddle-and-projectile target-clearing loop rather than a Neon Salvage extension. Whether it feels fun and whether the timing is well balanced remain human playtest questions.

## Criteria implemented

- Page presents the real name and one short drag instruction, with a visible objective, remaining time and score.
- Responsive portrait flex layout, reachable 46px buttons, local canvas drawing, no external assets, fonts, libraries, fetches, storage or services. Canvas alone uses `touch-action: none`; page controls retain native interaction.
- Stable `canvas`, `play`, `pause`, `restart`, `build-version` IDs. Source label remains `LOCAL BUILD`; JS never changes it. Runner must stamp the build before its gate.
- Start uses the native button click event; canceled canvas input never starts a game. Native buttons retain keyboard activation. No claim of verified trusted/canceled browser tap behavior is made.
- One primary pointer owns tray movement, subsequent pointers are ignored; release, cancellation and lost capture clear ownership. Left/right arrows and A/D move the same tray. Blur and document hiding pause running gameplay.
- Pause freezes actual simulation time and physics. Resume retains progress. Restart and end-screen Play again reset tiles, score, player, peach, clock, particles, held keys and pointer ownership, then start running.
- Frozen `window.BORHEZ_GAME` API returns new plain snapshots and nested player/peach objects from actual state. No writable diagnostics or fabricated test progress. Additional fields expose remaining targets and result.
- Reduced motion suppresses decorative jam particles. Essential peach motion remains so the game can be played.

## Executed checks and evidence

1. `node --check docs/games/studio-original-001/game.js` — passed, exit 0.
2. `node /tmp/peach-check.cjs` — final run passed all 11 checks. The temporary Node VM harness loads the actual production JS with DOM stubs; only its in-memory copy exposes internal functions/state for boundary setup. Production files and diagnostics are unchanged by this instrumentation. It checks:
   - Ready state, frozen API, snapshot mutation does not change player state.
   - Start handler enters running state and an actual update advances elapsed time.
   - A peach at (50,98) traveling upward intersects the first tile on the next 1/120-second update: score becomes 1, a repeat hit stays 1, and UI refresh shows `1 / 15`.
   - Pause freezes the complete snapshot through a simulated second; resume advances time.
   - Hitting each of the 15 unique real tiles triggers score 15, mode over and the success message.
   - Replay clears tile hits, timer, score and player position and starts running.
   - Advancing from 74.99 seconds past the limit clamps time to 75 and triggers the timeout ending.
   - A missed peach beyond the bottom respawns above the tray without adding score.
   - A downward peach crossing the tray changes to upward motion.
   - Primary pointer moves the tray, another pointer cannot take ownership, cancellation stops movement, and a new pointer can take ownership. Coordinate assertions allow floating point tolerance.
   - Restart also clears a held pointer and all progress.
   These prove production logic and handler behavior under controlled inputs, not browser event delivery, viewport usability or enjoyment. An initial exact-coordinate assertion differed by floating point rounding (220.00000000000003 versus 220); the harness now uses a 1e-9 tolerance. No game workaround was needed.
3. `wc -c docs/games/studio-original-001/index.html docs/games/studio-original-001/game.js docs/games/studio-original-001/game.css` — 1,079 + 7,652 + 1,592 = **10,323 bytes**, below 200,000.
4. `node game_factory/mobile_acceptance.cjs` — attempted, exit 1 before loading the page. Chromium failed at launch with `setsockopt: Operation not permitted`, SIGTRAP. The tool wrote its failure evidence to `artifacts/mobile/acceptance.json`. This is not a mobile acceptance pass or a gameplay failure diagnosis. No prior `artifacts/mobile/gate.log` existed. No tests were edited.
5. `node /tmp/peach-server.cjs` — temporary HTTP fixture attempted on 127.0.0.1:8765; sandbox rejected listen with EPERM. The fixture would have stamped the response build label only; it never served a page or changed the source label.
6. `git diff --stat` and `git status --short` — no tracked source modifications; only the new target directory appeared. Report/artifact files are ignored by repository status.

## Source fingerprints

`sha256sum` executed on the delivered source:

- index.html: `6b5d8df6198fc75f17cf4f3b7c9c09cb5f861ad30c87de5c5b0d9d0ab00bc1ca`
- game.js: `409af170603c1e9f88957a9d1fb7c211373629f118af911ac13404c10e7dc28c`
- game.css: `d2e00d5a81993138a1d609af584d1f8e0a93b6e6f51362a3e617f777e0736672`

## Remaining verification and delivery

The runner must execute the unchanged independent gate with its stamped build and supplied HTTP server, including 390x844 and 360x780 checks, then independent preview QA. This sandbox produced no browser screenshots or verified viewport results. Physical handset testing and subjective enjoyment are unverified. Automated internal tests do not establish session difficulty or every tile's practical reachability through normal player input.

Candidate host path is `/games/studio-original-001/`. Publication and exact live-file verification were not performed: this coding job permits editing only the target source and this report, while publishing code is explicitly out of scope. No public URL or independent QA approval is claimed. The later publication process should compare served files against accepted source, accounting for the runner's intentional HTML build-label stamp.
